answer: Client-side validation is a paradigm in which only the parties directly involved in a contract or transfer validate its state transitions off-chain, rather than every node on the network re-executing and storing the contract. The blockchain (Bitcoin) is used only to publish a compact cryptographic commitment and to prevent double-spending; it never sees or interprets the actual contract data. This is the inverse of ordinary blockchain validation, where global consensus nodes replicate and validate all state. It gives strong privacy (only counterparties see the data) and scalability (contract data is kept off the chain), at the cost of each participant having to keep and validate their own relevant history.
key_points: Only the parties involved validate state transitions, off-chain, not the whole network
The blockchain stores only a cryptographic commitment, not the contract data
Contrast: normal blockchains have every node replicate/validate/store all state (global validation)
Benefits: privacy (data seen only by counterparties) and scalability (data off-chain)
Each participant keeps and verifies only their own relevant shard/history

answer: A single-use seal is a cryptographic primitive analogous to a physical tamper-evident seal: it is a uniquely defined commitment point that can be 'closed' exactly once over a single message, producing publicly verifiable evidence of that closure. A secure single-use seal makes it computationally infeasible to produce two apparently valid proofs that the same seal was closed over two different messages. It is characterised by two operations: closing the seal over a message (which produces a witness/proof of closure) and verifying that a given seal was closed over a claimed message using that witness. Peter Todd introduced the concept in his 2016 'Commitments and Single-Use Seals' writeup.
key_points: Cryptographic analogue of a physical tamper-evident seal; can be closed exactly once over one message
Infeasible to produce two valid closures of the same seal over different messages (uniqueness/anti-double-spend)
Two operations: Close (seal over message -> witness) and Verify (seal, witness, message -> bool)
Closing produces a publicly verifiable witness/proof of closure
Introduced by Peter Todd (2016 'Commitments and Single-Use Seals')

answer: A specific Bitcoin transaction output (UTXO/txout) is globally unique and can be spent only once, which is exactly the 'closed once and only once' property a single-use seal needs. The seal definition is the chosen UTXO identified on-chain. The seal is closed by spending that UTXO in a transaction that also commits to the message (for example via an OP_RETURN or Taproot commitment carrying the message hash). The proof of publication is the fact that this spending transaction is confirmed in Bitcoin's consensus medium, so anyone can verify it. Bitcoin's double-spend prevention guarantees the UTXO cannot be spent again, so the seal cannot be validly closed over a second, different message.
key_points: A UTXO is globally unique and spendable only once
Seal definition = the specified UTXO/txout identified on-chain
Seal closing = spending that UTXO in a tx that commits to the message (e.g. via OP_RETURN or Taproot commitment)
Proof of publication = the confirmed spending transaction in Bitcoin's consensus/blockchain
Single-use property enforced by Bitcoin's double-spend prevention (cannot re-spend the UTXO)

answer: Proof of publication is the requirement that a message (or seal closure) is not merely committed to privately but is demonstrably published on a medium with global consensus properties, so that third parties can later verify it was made public. In the RGB/LNP-BP framing this is the 'proof-of-publication medium' — typically a blockchain such as Bitcoin — which makes it hard to forge, hide, or retroactively alter the fact that something was published. It is essential because single-use seals and client-side validation depend on the closure of a seal being publicly and immutably visible: without a trustworthy publication medium there would be no way to prove a seal was closed exactly once over a particular message, and equivocation could not be detected.
key_points: Proof that a message/seal-closure was publicly published, not just privately committed
Requires a medium with global consensus properties (e.g. Bitcoin blockchain) that makes forgery/retroactive change hard
Lets third parties verify publication and that a seal was closed exactly once
Underpins client-side validation and single-use seals; prevents undetected equivocation/double-closure
Concept originates with Peter Todd; formalised in RGB/LNP-BP as the publication medium

answer: A consignment is the off-chain data bundle that a sender transfers to a recipient so the recipient can validate the assets they are receiving. It contains the contract genesis, the relevant slice (DAG shard) of state transitions from genesis to the output being received, and the anchoring data (Bitcoin transaction ids and commitment proofs) needed to check the single-use seals. On receipt, the recipient validates the consignment client-side: it verifies every state transition against the contract schema, checks each anchor commitment against the Bitcoin blockchain, and confirms that each seal (UTXO) was closed exactly once with no conflicting transitions. There is no global RGB ledger, so the recipient only ever needs its own relevant history shard.
key_points: Off-chain data bundle sent from sender to recipient to validate a transfer
Contains genesis, the DAG shard of state transitions up to the received output, and anchor/commitment proofs
Recipient validates locally (client-side): checks transitions against the schema
Recipient verifies each anchor commitment against Bitcoin and that each seal was closed exactly once (no conflicts)
No global RGB ledger; only the relevant history shard is needed

answer: Tapret embeds the RGB commitment inside a Taproot output's script tree as a dedicated (unspendable) tapret script leaf, so the transaction looks like an ordinary Taproot spend and the commitment is hidden from casual observers. Opret instead places the commitment (e.g. a 32-byte hash) in the payload of an OP_RETURN output, which is provably unspendable and easily detectable but has a more visible footprint. The Deterministic Bitcoin Commitment (DBC) requirement is that a witness transaction must provably contain exactly one valid commitment per scheme: the only valid Opret commitment is in the FIRST OP_RETURN output, and the only valid Tapret commitment is in the FIRST Taproot output. This deterministic 'first-output' rule means an attacker cannot hide a second, conflicting RGB message elsewhere in the same transaction, so the message bound to a seal closure is unique.
key_points: Tapret: commitment placed in a Taproot output's script tree as a dedicated tapret leaf; looks like a normal Taproot spend (private)
Opret: commitment placed in an OP_RETURN output payload; provably unspendable but visible
DBC requires a transaction to provably contain exactly one valid commitment per scheme
Determinism rule: first OP_RETURN output (Opret) / first Taproot output (Tapret) is the only valid location
This prevents constructing alternative/conflicting commitment histories in the same transaction, keeping the seal-bound message unique

answer: AluVM (Algorithmic Logic Unit Virtual Machine) is a purely functional, register-based RISC virtual machine designed for deterministic, portable computation, created by Maxim Orlovsky and maintained by the LNP/BP Standards Association. It is the execution engine for RGB contract logic. Its key design choices are: it is register-based with no random (addressable) memory access; it has a reduced, orthogonal RISC-style instruction set; it is pure functional (no implicit side effects, I/O, or global mutable state); and instructions have fully defined semantics so there is no architecture-dependent undefined behaviour. Because RGB relies on client-side validation and cryptographic commitments, any non-determinism would break consensus — eliminating random memory access and undefined behaviour guarantees every validator computes identical results and makes the VM easier to reason about formally.
key_points: AluVM = Algorithmic Logic Unit VM: purely functional, register-based RISC virtual machine for deterministic portable computing
Created by Maxim Orlovsky, maintained by LNP/BP Standards Association; execution engine for RGB contracts
Register-based with NO random/addressable memory access
Pure functional: no side effects/I/O/global mutable state; reduced orthogonal instruction set
No undefined behaviour by design -> deterministic, so all client-side validators reach identical results (required for consensus)

answer: Contractum is a functional, declarative domain-specific language (still under development) for writing RGB smart contracts, with its design and compiler led by Maxim Orlovsky under the LNP/BP Standards Association. It uses the Strict Types formalism to define its data types, giving every type a fixed, deterministic, platform-independent binary encoding that can be validated at consensus level. A Contractum program compiles down into the RGB artefacts needed to run a contract — schema, interfaces and interface implementations, genesis and contract operations — together with AluVM bytecode, which is the executable logic that RGB validators run. So Contractum is the high-level authoring layer, Strict Types is its deterministic type/encoding system, and AluVM is the deterministic execution target.
key_points: Contractum: functional/declarative DSL for writing RGB smart contracts (work in progress)
Designed/led by Maxim Orlovsky under the LNP/BP Standards Association
Uses Strict Types formalism for data types -> fixed, deterministic, platform-independent binary encoding
Compiles to RGB schema, interfaces/implementations, genesis, contract operations
Compiles to AluVM bytecode as the execution target (high-level language -> AluVM)

answer: Bifrost is an extensible Lightning-network protocol defined by a group of LNPBP standards (notably LNPBP-50 for the P2P layer and LNPBP-51 for channels) that serves as the transport and channel layer for RGB and other client-side-validated protocols over Lightning. It reuses the Noise_XK handshake and framing ideas from BOLT-8 (re-standardised as LNPBP-15/LNPBP-18) but replaces BOLT's message formats with Strict-Types-encoded messages and richer channel semantics. It exists because standard BOLT Lightning does not natively support the deterministic commitments, single-use seals, Taproot/MuSig-based channels, or multi-peer channel structures that RGB needs; Bifrost provides those, so RGB assets can be carried over Lightning-style channels. Bifrost channels that carry such protocols cannot be downgraded back to legacy BOLT channels.
key_points: Bifrost = extensible Lightning protocol defined by LNPBP standards (LNPBP-50 P2P, LNPBP-51 channels)
Transport/channel layer enabling RGB (and other client-side-validated protocols) over Lightning
Reuses Noise_XK/framing from BOLT-8 (as LNPBP-15/18) but uses Strict-Types encoding instead of BOLT TLV
Solves what BOLT can't: native deterministic commitments, single-use seals, Taproot/MuSig, multi-peer channels
Bifrost channels carrying these protocols cannot be downgraded to legacy BOLT channels

answer: The LNP/BP Standards Association is a Swiss non-profit association that supervises and maintains open standards and reference implementations for Bitcoin Layer 2 and Layer 3 protocols, including RGB, Bifrost, and related technologies, and manages the RGB consensus layer and its governance. The LNPBP standards ('Lightning Network Protocol / Bitcoin Protocol' standards) are a family of formal specifications for primitives and protocols that anchor to Bitcoin via deterministic commitments without requiring any Bitcoin soft/hard fork and are not already covered by the Lightning BOLTs. Examples include LNPBP-1/2/3 (public-key, script and deterministic transaction-output commitments), LNPBP-8 (single-use seals), LNPBP-12 (Tapret), and the RGB interface standards. Key figures include Maxim Orlovsky (technical lead of RGB/AluVM/Contractum) and Giacomo Zucco, who was involved in the early conception of RGB.
key_points: Swiss non-profit association maintaining open standards and reference implementations for Bitcoin L2/L3 (RGB, Bifrost, etc.)
Manages the RGB consensus layer and governance
LNPBP standards = specs for Bitcoin-anchored primitives/protocols needing no Bitcoin fork, not covered by BOLTs
Examples: LNPBP-1/2/3 commitments, LNPBP-8 single-use seals, LNPBP-12 Tapret, RGB interfaces
Key people: Maxim Orlovsky (RGB/AluVM/Contractum lead) and Giacomo Zucco (early RGB)

answer: Taproot Assets, a Lightning Labs protocol, issues assets by committing asset state into a Taproot output: the output's internal key is tweaked to commit to the root of a Merkle-Sum Sparse Merkle Tree (MS-SMT) describing the asset, so on-chain the UTXO looks like an ordinary P2TR output. An MS-SMT is a sparse Merkle tree (a 256-level authenticated key-value map supporting inclusion and non-inclusion proofs) in which every leaf carries a numeric amount and every internal node carries the sum of its children, so the root sum equals total supply and transfers can be checked for supply conservation. Asset IDs are derived deterministically from the genesis outpoint plus metadata. Like RGB it uses client-side validation, with receivers verifying an off-chain proof chain from genesis. It differs from RGB in that it is standardised around Taproot commitments and the specific MS-SMT data structure (draft bip-tap BIPs) and is tightly integrated with Lightning Labs' Lightning stack, whereas RGB uses its own AluVM/Strict-Types VM, single-use-seal anchoring (Tapret/Opret), and different Merkle data structures.
key_points: Taproot Assets (Lightning Labs) commits asset state into a Taproot output via a tweaked key; on-chain it looks like a normal P2TR spend
MS-SMT = sparse Merkle tree (inclusion + non-inclusion proofs) where leaves carry amounts and nodes carry sums
Root sum = total supply, enabling supply-conservation / non-inflation proofs; asset ID derived from genesis outpoint + metadata
Also uses client-side validation: receivers verify an off-chain proof chain from genesis
Vs RGB: standardised on Taproot + MS-SMT (bip-tap) and Lightning Labs LN, whereas RGB uses AluVM/Strict Types, single-use-seal Tapret/Opret anchoring and different data structures

answer: Ordinal theory (Casey Rodarmor) assigns every satoshi a serial number in the order it is mined in coinbase transactions — the first sat of the genesis block is 0 and the last is 4,999,999,999 — and tracks sats as they move using a first-in-first-out rule mapping input sats to output sats; Bitcoin itself is unaware of these numbers, which are computed off-chain by an indexer. An inscription attaches arbitrary data to a sat by placing it in the witness of a Taproot script-path spend, inside an 'envelope': an unexecuted OP_FALSE OP_IF ... OP_ENDIF branch containing data pushes (the 'ord' identifier, a content-type/MIME tag, and the body), which never executes and so does not affect script validity but is recorded on-chain (benefiting from the segwit witness discount). BRC-20 (introduced by the pseudonymous Domo in March 2023) is a convention that inscribes JSON with deploy/mint/transfer operations (fields like p, op, tick, max, lim, amt); it is described as an off-chain, indexer-based experiment because Bitcoin enforces none of its rules — balances exist only because off-chain indexers replay the inscriptions by an agreed convention, so there is no consensus-level standard and indexers can diverge.
key_points: Ordinal theory (Casey Rodarmor) numbers sats by mining order; genesis block sats run 0 to 4,999,999,999; transfers tracked FIFO; Bitcoin is unaware (off-chain indexer)
Inscription = data in the witness of a Taproot script-path spend inside an OP_FALSE OP_IF ... OP_ENDIF 'envelope'
Envelope holds 'ord' identifier, content-type/MIME tag and body; branch never executes (no effect on validity) but is stored on-chain; uses segwit witness discount
BRC-20 by Domo (March 2023): JSON inscriptions with deploy/mint/transfer ops (p, op, tick, max, lim, amt)
Off-chain/indexer-based: Bitcoin enforces no BRC-20 rules; balances computed by indexers replaying inscriptions; no BIP/consensus standard, indexers can diverge

answer: A Solid Pod (Personal Online Data Store) is a user-controlled web storage space, addressed by an HTTP(S) base URL, in which a person keeps their data as resources and decides who may read or write it. Solid decouples applications from data: instead of each app storing your data on its own backend and locking it in, apps request permissioned access to data that lives in your Pod, so the same data can be reused across many apps and you retain ownership and portability. A Pod can be hosted anywhere (a commercial provider, a personal server, or a self-hosted instance), and the Pod owner is identified by a WebID that holds authority over access control for that storage. The core problem it addresses is application-centric data silos and the loss of user control and portability on the conventional web.
key_points: A Pod is a user-controlled personal online data store accessed over HTTP(S)
Solid decouples/separates data from the applications that use it
It targets data lock-in, silos, and lack of ownership/portability
A Pod can be hosted anywhere and owned/controlled by its user
The Pod owner is identified by a WebID that governs access

answer: A Solid Pod implements (parts of) the W3C Linked Data Platform (LDP) as its HTTP interaction model: resources and LDP containers are read and written with standard HTTP verbs (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE), with RDF resources typically serialised as Turtle or JSON-LD. For authorisation Solid supports two models. Web Access Control (WAC) is ACL-based: each protected resource has an associated ACL resource (RDF) listing authorisations that bind agents (WebIDs, groups, or the public) to access modes (acl:Read, acl:Write, acl:Append, acl:Control), with default/inheritable ACLs walked up the container hierarchy when a resource has no ACL of its own. Access Control Policies (ACP) is a newer, more expressive policy language: each resource has an Access Control Resource containing Policies and Matchers, where matchers describe conditions (e.g. which agent or client) and policies allow or deny modes, granting a mode only if at least one policy allows it and none deny it. WAC is the classic ACL model; ACP separates matching conditions from allow/deny policy statements for richer, context-aware control.
key_points: Pods implement the W3C Linked Data Platform (LDP) over HTTP with containers and standard verbs
WAC is ACL-based with per-resource ACL resources in RDF
WAC access modes are Read, Write, Append, Control, plus inheritable/default ACLs
ACP uses Access Control Resources with Policies and Matchers
ACP grants a mode only if a policy allows and none deny; it is more expressive/context-aware

answer: Solid-OIDC is a profile of OpenID Connect (built on the OIDC authorization code flow and OAuth 2.0) that adapts it to Solid's decentralised identity model. Its key additions are: a 'webid' scope/claim, so the issued ID Token carries a 'webid' claim equal to the user's WebID URI; issuer discovery driven by the WebID Profile rather than a fixed provider, where a client learns the acceptable OpenID Providers by reading solid:oidcIssuer triples from the WebID document; and mandatory DPoP-bound tokens. DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession, RFC 9449) requires the client to sign a DPoP proof JWT with a private key it holds; the OP issues tokens bound to that key's thumbprint. On every request to a Pod the client sends the token plus a fresh DPoP proof (carrying htm, htu, iat, jti, and an access-token hash) signed with the same key, so a resource server can confirm the caller holds the key the token is bound to. Combined with the WebID profile endorsing the issuer, this cryptographically proves the caller legitimately acts for the WebID named in the token.
key_points: Solid-OIDC is a profile/extension of OpenID Connect / OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow
It adds a 'webid' scope and a 'webid' claim in the ID Token equal to the user's WebID
Issuer discovery uses solid:oidcIssuer triples in the WebID profile, not a fixed provider
DPoP (RFC 9449) binds tokens to a client-held key via proof-of-possession JWTs
Each request sends a fresh DPoP proof so the Pod verifies the caller holds the bound key

answer: The client discovers the acceptable issuer(s) by dereferencing the WebID URI and inspecting the returned RDF profile document for triples using the predicate http://www.w3.org/ns/solid/terms#oidcIssuer (i.e. solid:oidcIssuer). The object of each such triple is the URL of an OpenID Provider that the WebID's controller has authorised to issue tokens for that WebID. Because this authoritative list lives in the WebID document, which is under the control of the identity's owner, the trust relationship is decentralised: any provider can serve any user, but a relying party accepts an ID Token only if its issuer matches one listed in that WebID's profile. The client then runs the standard OIDC flow against the discovered issuer.
key_points: The client dereferences the WebID URI to fetch its RDF profile document
It looks for solid:oidcIssuer (http://www.w3.org/ns/solid/terms#oidcIssuer) triples
The object of each triple names an authorised OpenID Provider for that WebID
The WebID owner controls this list, keeping issuer trust decentralised
A relying party accepts a token only if its issuer matches one listed in the profile

answer: A WebID is an HTTP(S) URI that acts as a globally unique identifier for an agent, typically a person but also an organisation, application or device. It is more than a plain URL because dereferencing it (via HTTP GET on its document part) returns a WebID Profile Document expressed in RDF, commonly Turtle, that describes the agent and, crucially, holds authentication material such as public key(s) or the identity provider(s) trusted for that agent. A WebID usually takes the form of a URL with a fragment, e.g. https://example.org/profile#me, where the document lives at the fragmentless URL and the fragment identifies the RDF node denoting the agent. This binding of a self-hosted URI to a machine-readable, owner-controlled RDF profile is what lets WebID serve as a decentralised identity mechanism where each person controls their own identifier and description.
key_points: A WebID is an HTTP(S) URI identifying an agent (person, org, app, device)
Dereferencing it returns an RDF WebID Profile Document (often Turtle)
It typically uses a fragment (e.g. #me) so the URI denotes the agent node in the document
The profile holds identity/auth material such as public keys or trusted issuers
The owner controls their own identifier and profile, enabling decentralised identity

answer: Both protocols end in the same result: a relying party gains a WebID URI whose control by the connecting agent has been verified. WebID-TLS operates at the TLS layer using mutual TLS with a client X.509 certificate: the certificate's Subject Alternative Name carries the WebID URI, the server extracts it, dereferences the WebID profile, and checks that the public key in the certificate matches a public key stated in that RDF profile, proving the client controls the WebID. WebID-OIDC instead operates at the application layer, reusing OpenID Connect/OAuth2: an identity provider issues an ID Token from which the WebID URI is obtained (and, in Solid, the profile's solid:oidcIssuer list confirms the provider is authorised). The ecosystem shifted to WebID-OIDC (and its successor Solid-OIDC) chiefly because mutual TLS with client certificates has poor browser and UX support, whereas OIDC/OAuth2 redirect-and-token flows are widely deployed, more usable, and let holders freely choose their own identity provider.
key_points: Both yield a verified WebID URI the agent is proven to control
WebID-TLS uses mutual TLS with a client X.509 cert carrying the WebID in its Subject Alternative Name
WebID-TLS verifies the cert's public key against a key in the WebID RDF profile
WebID-OIDC works at the application layer via OpenID Connect ID Tokens
The move happened because client-certificate mTLS has poor browser/UX support while OIDC is widely deployed and lets holders pick their IdP

answer: The WebID Profile Document is the RDF document retrieved by dereferencing the document part of a WebID URI. Usually written in Turtle (though any RDF serialisation is acceptable), it describes the agent and normally contains a foaf:primaryTopic link to the WebID node plus the authentication-relevant metadata: one or more public keys and, in OIDC-based flows, the trusted issuer(s). During authentication a relying party dereferences the WebID, parses the RDF, and uses that data to verify control of the identity: in WebID-TLS it matches the certificate's public key against a key in the profile, and in WebID-OIDC/Solid-OIDC it reads solid:oidcIssuer to confirm the ID Token came from an authorised provider. Because the profile is hosted and edited only by its owner, it is the self-managed, authoritative source of truth for the identity's keys and delegation.
key_points: It is the RDF (typically Turtle) document returned by dereferencing the WebID
It describes the agent and links the document to the WebID node (e.g. foaf:primaryTopic)
It holds authentication material: public key(s) and/or trusted issuer(s)
In WebID-TLS it supplies the key matched against the client certificate; in OIDC it supplies solid:oidcIssuer
It is owner-controlled, making it the authoritative source of truth for the identity

answer: NIP-01 defines every piece of Nostr data as a single event object with the fields: id (a 32-byte hex identifier), pubkey (the author's 32-byte secp256k1 public key in hex), created_at (a Unix timestamp in seconds), kind (an integer denoting the event type, e.g. 0 for metadata, 1 for a short text note), tags (an array of tag arrays for references and metadata), content (an arbitrary UTF-8 string whose meaning depends on kind), and sig (a Schnorr signature). The id is the lowercase-hex SHA-256 hash of the canonical serialisation, a JSON array [0, pubkey, created_at, kind, tags, content]. Integrity is guaranteed because altering any field changes that hash and therefore the id; authorship is guaranteed because sig is a Schnorr signature over the id using secp256k1, which only the holder of the corresponding private key can produce and anyone can verify against the pubkey. NIP-01 also defines the WebSocket client-relay messages (EVENT, REQ, CLOSE from clients; EVENT, OK, EOSE, NOTICE, CLOSED from relays).
key_points: Event fields: id, pubkey, created_at, kind, tags, content, sig
pubkey is a 32-byte secp256k1 key; kind is an integer type (0 metadata, 1 text note)
id is the SHA-256 hash of the canonical serialisation [0,pubkey,created_at,kind,tags,content]
sig is a Schnorr signature over the id using secp256k1, verifiable against the pubkey
Any change alters the id/signature; NIP-01 also defines the WebSocket EVENT/REQ/CLOSE and EVENT/OK/EOSE/NOTICE messages

answer: NIP-19 defines bech32-formatted, human-friendly encodings of Nostr entities. 'npub' encodes a 32-byte secp256k1 public key and 'nsec' encodes the corresponding 32-byte private key; 'note' encodes an event id, while TLV-based forms like nprofile, nevent, naddr bundle a key or event id together with extra data such as relay hints. Their purpose is purely presentational: readable display, copy-paste, and QR codes. NIP-19 explicitly states these bech32 strings MUST NOT appear inside NIP-01 events or subscription filters, which use the canonical raw hex (or binary) form; clients should accept npub/nsec on input, convert them internally to hex, and only put hex on the wire. This separation keeps the protocol's core data model unambiguous while giving users a friendlier surface form.
key_points: NIP-19 defines bech32 encodings for Nostr entities
npub encodes a public key; nsec encodes a private key; note encodes an event id
TLV forms (nprofile, nevent, naddr) add extra data like relay hints
They are for human display/copy-paste/QR only
They MUST NOT be used inside NIP-01 events or filters, which use canonical hex; clients convert on input

answer: The did:nostr method makes a Nostr public key itself the identifier: a DID has the form did:nostr:<identifier> where the identifier is derived directly from the 32-byte Nostr secp256k1 public key. There is no registry, ledger, or minting step, the keypair already used on Nostr resolves straight to a DID Document. Resolution is offline-first and deterministic: a minimal DID Document can be built from the key alone, containing the DID as id and a verificationMethod (of type Multikey, using publicKeyMultibase) controlled by that DID, aligned with W3C DID Core and Controlled Identifiers. Optionally the resolver can query Nostr relays for the pubkey's kind-0 metadata and related events to enrich the document with services, alsoKnownAs, or other properties, but network data is only supplemental and never required. This differs from ledger/blockchain-anchored methods (e.g. did:ion, did:ethr) in that it needs no distributed ledger, on-chain transaction, or global consensus; control of the DID is simply possession of the Nostr private key, the same root of trust as signing Nostr events.
key_points: A did:nostr DID maps directly to a Nostr secp256k1 public key: did:nostr:<pubkey>
No registry, ledger, or minting step is required
Resolution is offline-first/deterministic: a minimal DID Document is built from the key alone
The verificationMethod uses Multikey / publicKeyMultibase, per W3C DID Core and Controlled Identifiers
Nostr relays can optionally enrich the document (kind-0 metadata) but are not required; control = holding the private key, unlike ledger-based methods

answer: Git is a content-addressed store whose object graph is a Merkle DAG. File contents are stored as blobs named by the cryptographic hash of their content (SHA-1 historically, with SHA-256 support added), directories as tree objects that hash the list of names and child object hashes, and each commit hashes its root tree, its parent commit(s), and its metadata. Because every identifier is the hash of its content, changing a file changes its blob hash, which changes the enclosing tree hash, which changes the commit hash, and rewriting history changes the parent links and hence every downstream commit id, so any tampering is detectable by recomputing hashes. ('Git-Mark' is not a standard Git term; it denotes this pattern of using commit hashes as anchors for a document trail.) The key limitation is that a Git commit's timestamp is just self-asserted local metadata and can be forged or back-dated; Git proves what changed relative to prior state but not independently when it existed. That is why provenance systems anchor a commit hash (or document hash) into an external, trusted timestamping layer such as a public blockchain, adding a proof of existence that does not rely on the repository's own clock.
key_points: Git is content-addressed: blobs, trees, and commits are named by cryptographic hashes
The commit graph is a Merkle DAG; a commit hashes its tree, parent(s), and metadata
Any content change or history rewrite changes hashes, making tampering detectable
Git commit timestamps are self-asserted local metadata and can be forged/back-dated
So commit or document hashes are anchored externally (e.g. a blockchain) for trusted proof-of-existence; 'Git-Mark' is a pattern name, not a Git feature

answer: OpenTimestamps produces a proof of existence by anchoring a document's hash to a blockchain, usually Bitcoin, without ever revealing the document. The user hashes the document locally (SHA-256) and submits only that digest to public calendar servers. A calendar aggregates many submitted digests as leaves of a Merkle tree, computing a single Merkle root that commits to all of them, and periodically writes that root into a Bitcoin transaction (e.g. in an OP_RETURN output). Once the transaction is mined and confirmed, the root is permanently recorded in a block whose header carries a timestamp. The user receives a compact .ots proof file containing the document hash, the Merkle path of sibling hashes from the leaf up to the root, and the attestation linking that root to a specific Bitcoin block. To verify, one recomputes the document's hash, walks the Merkle path to reconstruct the root, and checks it is committed in the referenced block. The proof demonstrates that the document existed at or before that block's time (it could not be back-dated without rewriting proof-of-work history) and that the document is unaltered (any change breaks the hash match). Verification is trust-minimised: it depends only on the document, the .ots file, and public Bitcoin block headers, not on trusting the calendar server, and Merkle aggregation lets a single transaction timestamp thousands of documents at once.
key_points: Only the document's SHA-256 hash is submitted; the document never leaves the user
Calendar servers aggregate many hashes into a Merkle tree and anchor the Merkle root in a Bitcoin transaction (e.g. OP_RETURN)
The .ots proof holds the hash, the Merkle path, and the attestation to a specific block
Verification recomputes the hash, walks the Merkle path, and checks the block, proving existence-before-time and tamper-evidence
Trust-minimised: relies only on the document, proof file, and public block headers; one transaction timestamps many documents

answer: Git's four object types — blob, tree, commit and tag — are each stored under an object ID that is the cryptographic hash of the object's exact serialised content, i.e. content addressing (git-scm: 'All objects are named by the SHA-1 hash of their contents ... globally unique'). Objects embed the IDs of other objects: a commit names its root tree and parent commit(s) by hash; a tree names its blobs and sub-trees by hash; a tag names its target by hash. Because every edge is the hash of the target object, the links are authenticated Merkle links, forming a directed acyclic graph (a Merkle DAG), not a linear chain — a commit fans out to a whole tree of trees and blobs. It is acyclic because an object's ID is fixed by its content: you cannot make object A reference a not-yet-existing hash of B that in turn references A, since changing content produces a new hash and hence a new object rather than mutating the target in place.
key_points: Four object types: blob, tree, commit, tag
Object ID = cryptographic hash of the object's serialised content (content addressing)
Edges are hashes of target objects (Merkle links), so links are authenticated
DAG, not a chain: commits fan out to trees which fan out to blobs/sub-trees
Acyclic because content determines the hash — you cannot embed a hash of an object that embeds you

answer: A transition-era repository uses core.repositoryFormatVersion = 1 with extensions.objectFormat = sha256 (the storage hash, which determines the 64-hex-digit object IDs) and extensions.compatObjectFormat = sha1 (a compatibility hash that must differ from objectFormat). To make objects addressable under both algorithms, a SHA-256 repository stores a bidirectional mapping between SHA-256 and SHA-1 object names alongside the packfile, so objects can be named by either their 40-hex SHA-1 or 64-hex SHA-256 IDs. SHA-1 remains the default object format, SHA-256 support is still marked experimental, and there is presently no general interoperability between SHA-256 and SHA-1 repositories — they cannot share work and old Git versions cannot read a SHA-256 repository. Git's BreakingChanges plan intends to eventually switch the default for new repositories to SHA-256 once ecosystem support is sufficient, but there is no plan to deprecate the SHA-1 object format.
key_points: objectFormat = the storage hash (sha256 => 64-hex object IDs); default is sha1
compatObjectFormat = a compatibility hash, must differ from objectFormat, for format-1 interop testing
SHA-256 repos store a bidirectional SHA-256<->SHA-1 name mapping beside the packfile
Objects can be named by 40-hex SHA-1 or 64-hex SHA-256 IDs
No interoperability today; SHA-256 support is experimental; old Git cannot read SHA-256 repos
Planned default switch to SHA-256 later; SHA-1 format not being deprecated

answer: Modern Git builds do not use plain SHA-1; they use a hardened SHA-1 implementation, sha1dc (SHA-1 collision detection, by Stevens and Shumow), as the default hash. sha1dc computes the ordinary SHA-1 digest but simultaneously runs a detection algorithm that watches for the specific disturbance-vector / message-block patterns characteristic of a SHA-1 collision attack (the identical-prefix collision technique used by SHAttered). If such a pattern is detected it aborts rather than emitting a digest, so a crafted colliding object is rejected. This mitigates the known collision constructions cheaply, but it is a stop-gap: it does not make SHA-1 collision-resistant against future novel attacks, which is why Git is separately building out the SHA-256 object format. sha1dc is an implementation-level defence and is complementary to, not a substitute for, the architectural move to SHA-256.
key_points: Git uses hardened SHA-1 = sha1dc (collision-detecting SHA-1), not plain SHA-1, by default
sha1dc detects the disturbance-vector/message-block signatures of known SHA-1 collision attacks
It aborts instead of returning a digest when an attack pattern is seen, rejecting crafted colliding objects
Mitigates SHAttered-style identical-prefix collisions cheaply
It is a stop-gap; does not restore general collision resistance — hence the parallel SHA-256 transition

answer: A signed commit binds a specific signing key to the exact hashed commit payload: the signature (stored in the gpgsig header) covers the commit object — its tree, parent(s), author/committer identities and message — so any alteration invalidates it, verifiable with git verify-commit or git log --show-signature. That is an authenticity/integrity guarantee ('this key endorsed this content'), not a trusted-time guarantee. The commit's author and committer date fields are simply attacker-controllable strings set by the client; nothing in the signature attests that the commit really existed at that moment, and back- or forward-dating is trivial. To obtain a trustworthy 'existed no later than T' you need an external anchor — e.g. an OpenTimestamps proof anchoring the commit hash to a Bitcoin block, or a transparency-log inclusion — because only a third party with independent time (a blockchain, a log, a timestamping authority) can bound existence in time.
key_points: Signed commit = key binds to the hashed commit object (tree, parents, identities, message) via the gpgsig header
Provides authenticity/integrity, verifiable with git verify-commit / git log --show-signature
The author/committer date fields are client-set and attacker-controllable — not attested by the signature
Signatures give no trusted time; back-/forward-dating is trivial
A trusted 'existed before T' needs an external anchor (OpenTimestamps/blockchain or a transparency log)

answer: A git note is itself a blob (extra information supplementing an object, usually a commit), stored not inside the target commit but in a separate notes ref — by default refs/notes/commits — whose tree maps target object names (paths) to the note blobs. Because the note lives in an independent ref rather than in the commit object, the annotated commit's serialised content, and therefore its object ID, is unchanged; this is precisely why notes can be added, edited or removed after the fact and can annotate immutable, even signed, commits. The trade-off is that notes are not covered by a signature over the original commit: the note ref has its own separate Git history (its own hash chain) that can itself be signed or protected, but a signature on the commit does not vouch for its notes. So notes are a good place to record provenance pointers — e.g. the ID or hash of an OpenTimestamps .ots proof for the commit — provided you separately protect the notes ref, since the annotation's integrity is independent of the commit's.
key_points: A note is a blob stored in a separate notes ref (default refs/notes/commits), keyed by target object name
The commit object is not modified, so its object ID stays the same — hence notes can annotate immutable/signed commits
Notes are mutable after the fact (add/edit/remove) precisely because they are external to the commit
A signature over the commit does NOT cover its notes; the notes ref has its own hash chain
Good for carrying provenance pointers (e.g. an .ots proof ID) but the notes ref must be protected/signed separately

answer: Clients submit only the hash of a document to a calendar server. The calendar aggregates every request received in the same short interval (about one second) into a single Merkle tree, whose tip (root) is one 32-byte digest committing to all those documents at once; each client gets back a proof consisting of the operations (sibling hashes) climbing from its document hash to that tip — which is why one Bitcoin transaction can anchor unlimited documents. The calendar's job is a trust compromise: it must ensure every aggregated tip is eventually anchored on Bitcoin and keep the completed proofs available, but it need not be trusted for correctness because the finished proof verifies entirely against the blockchain. As for reaching Bitcoin: per Peter Todd, the calendar creates a Bitcoin transaction that commits to that single 32-byte tip, and the currently deployed calendar servers embed the digest directly in an OP_RETURN output. That transaction is then itself a leaf of the block's transaction Merkle tree, so the block header's merkleroot is the ultimate commitment — but the specific mechanism to get the digest into the block today is OP_RETURN, not (yet) a subtler tx-structure commitment (an alternative Poelstra scheme exists as a 2017 PR but is not in the standard protocol).
key_points: Clients send only a document hash; requests in a ~1-second interval are aggregated into one Merkle tree
The tree tip is a single 32-byte digest; each client's proof is the sibling-hash path from its hash to the tip
One Bitcoin transaction thus anchors an unlimited number of documents
Calendars must anchor tips and keep proofs available, but need not be trusted — proofs verify against the blockchain
Deployed calendars embed the tip directly in an OP_RETURN output (per Peter Todd)
The block header's transaction merkleroot is the ultimate commitment; the alternative non-OP_RETURN scheme is not in the standard protocol

answer: git-mark (invoked as `git mark`, distributed via npm) anchors Git commits onto a supporting blockchain (Bitmark, framed as Bitcoin-like) to create an auditable, tamper-proof record. On first use you bind the repository to a genesis unspent transaction with `git mark --genesis txid:output`; this fixes the starting point of a per-repository chain of mark transactions. Each subsequent `git mark` advances that chain by creating a new blockchain transaction that commits to the current Git HEAD commit hash plus metadata, so once the block confirms, that commit state is anchored under public consensus and cannot be rewritten without contradicting the ledger. The difference in guarantee is the external anchor: Git's own hash chain plus signed commits only prove internal integrity and author endorsement — they are tamper-evident merely relative to another copy of the repo, and a force-push can rewrite history undetectably if no external reference exists. Anchoring the HEAD hash to a blockchain moves the guarantee from 'tamper-evident within Git' to 'tamper-evident against a global, time-ordered consensus ledger', giving proof of existence and state at a confirmed block time.
key_points: git-mark (`git mark`, via npm) anchors commit hashes to a supporting blockchain (Bitmark)
`git mark --genesis txid:output` binds the repo to a genesis unspent transaction, starting a mark chain
Each `git mark` creates a new tx committing to the current HEAD commit hash + metadata; block confirmation anchors it
Git's hash chain + signed commits give only internal integrity/authenticity, tamper-evident relative to another copy
A force-push can rewrite history undetectably without an external reference; the blockchain anchor removes that gap
Result: proof of existence/state against a global consensus ledger, not just within Git

answer: The OpenTimestamps client hooks into Git by wrapping the GPG program that Git invokes when signing. It provides an ots-git-gpg-wrapper (with a shell entry point ots-git-gpg-wrapper.sh); you activate it with `git config --global gpg.program <path to ots-git-gpg-wrapper.sh>`. Thereafter `git commit -S` calls the wrapper instead of GPG directly: the wrapper produces the normal commit signature via GPG and additionally creates an OpenTimestamps proof that anchors the commit/signature to Bitcoin through the calendar servers (with options such as --wait to block until the timestamp is upgraded). The problem this solves is temporal: an ordinary signed commit only proves 'this key signed this content', with no trustworthy time. If the signing key is later revoked, expired or compromised, a plain signature becomes ambiguous — you cannot tell whether it was made while the key was still valid. The Bitcoin-anchored timestamp proves the signature existed before a specific block time, i.e. before the revocation, letting verifiers still trust signatures that pre-date a key's compromise.
key_points: Integration wraps the GPG program Git calls: ots-git-gpg-wrapper (ots-git-gpg-wrapper.sh)
Activated via `git config gpg.program <wrapper>` (typically --global)
On `git commit -S` the wrapper both produces the GPG signature and creates an OTS proof anchoring to Bitcoin via calendars
A plain signed commit proves only 'key signed content', with no trustworthy time
Anchoring proves the signature existed before a given block time — crucial once a key is revoked/expired/compromised
Lets verifiers still trust signatures that pre-date a key's compromise

answer: RFC 6962 builds a binary Merkle tree over an ordered list of entries using SHA-256. For a single-entry list the leaf hash is MTH({d[0]}) = SHA-256(0x00 || d[0]). For n > 1, letting k be the largest power of two strictly less than n, the interior node is MTH(D[n]) = SHA-256(0x01 || MTH(D[0:k]) || MTH(D[k:n])). The distinct prefix bytes 0x00 (leaf) and 0x01 (interior) implement domain separation: the input spaces of leaf hashes and interior-node hashes are made disjoint, so no leaf hash can ever equal an interior-node hash. This blocks second-preimage / tree-structure ambiguity attacks in which an adversary would present a leaf whose value coincides with the concatenation of two child hashes (or vice versa), thereby forging a different tree shape that hashes to the same root. Without the prefixes such a structural collision would be possible even though SHA-256 itself is collision-resistant.
key_points: Interior (n>1, k = largest power of two < n): MTH = SHA-256(0x01 || MTH(D[0:k]) || MTH(D[k:n]))
0x00 vs 0x01 = domain separation making leaf and interior hash inputs disjoint
No leaf hash can collide with an interior-node hash
Prevents second-preimage / tree-reshaping attacks where a leaf value mimics a child-hash concatenation
Needed because such structural ambiguity would exist even with a collision-resistant SHA-256

answer: An audit path (inclusion proof) proves that one specific leaf is present in a tree of a given size: given the leaf hash, the list of sibling hashes up to the root, and the root hash from a Signed Tree Head, the verifier recomputes the root and checks it matches — it proves membership of a single item. A consistency proof instead proves the append-only property between two tree states: given two STHs of sizes m <= n, it is the minimal set of node hashes needed to show the smaller tree of size m is a prefix of the larger tree of size n, i.e. that nothing was deleted or rewritten, only appended. A Signed Tree Head is the log's signed commitment to its current state, containing the tree size, the root (tree-head) hash, a timestamp and the log's signature (plus log-identifying metadata). The Maximum Merge Delay (MMD) is a log-declared time bound within which any accepted certificate must be incorporated into the tree and covered by a new STH; a client can therefore demand an inclusion proof against any STH dated after SCT-timestamp + MMD, and a log that fails to honour its MMD is treated as misbehaving.
key_points: Inclusion/audit proof: sibling hashes from a leaf to the root; proves one leaf is in the tree of a given STH
Consistency proof: node hashes proving tree of size m is a prefix of tree of size n (m<=n) — append-only, nothing deleted/altered
Inclusion needs leaf hash + audit path + STH root; consistency needs two STH roots/sizes + consistency path
STH contains: tree size, root (tree-head) hash, timestamp, log signature (and log ID metadata)
MMD = log-declared max time to incorporate an accepted cert into the tree and cover it with an STH
Client verifies inclusion against an STH dated after SCT timestamp + MMD; failing MMD = misbehaviour

answer: Trillian core is a generic, storage-backed append-only Merkle tree that provides sequencing and inclusion/consistency proofs but no application semantics. A personality is the application layer built on top of that core for a specific kind of log (a CT log, a key-transparency log, a software-supply-chain log, etc.), and it owns three responsibilities the core intentionally omits: (1) admission criteria — deciding what may be logged (e.g. only valid X.509 certificates); (2) canonicalisation — mapping equivalent submissions to a canonical form so the core can de-duplicate; and (3) the external interface — the client-facing API, ACLs, rate-limiting and DoS protection, which it translates into core operations like QueueLeaf and GetInclusionProof. A tile, in tile-based logs, is a fixed-size subtree of Merkle nodes (a group of hashes) stored and served as one unit; tiling batches the tree's hashes so that storage, recomputation and proof-serving read a small number of tiles rather than walking individual nodes, greatly reducing per-request overhead and making the log cheap to serve and mirror.
key_points: Trillian core = generic storage-backed append-only Merkle tree with inclusion/consistency proofs, no app semantics
A personality = the application layer for a specific log type on top of the core
Personality owns: (1) admission criteria (what may be logged)
(2) canonicalisation (equivalent submissions -> canonical form for de-duplication)
(3) external interface/API, ACLs, rate-limiting/DoS; maps to core ops like QueueLeaf/GetInclusionProof
A tile = a fixed-size subtree/group of Merkle hashes stored and served as one unit; tiling cuts storage/recompute/proof-serving overhead and eases mirroring

answer: AluVM is a register-based (no random-access memory), purely functional RISC VM. Its integer arithmetic 'A' registers are organised as 8 blocks of 32 registers each, of widths 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512 and 1024 bits; there are large 'R' registers reserved for cryptography (elliptic-curve/hashing) and a single block of 256 'S' string registers of up to 64 KiB each, plus control registers headed by the boolean status register st0. Exception-freedom comes from making every register nullable: any impossible, invalid or type-mismatched operation does not trap — it simply sets the destination register to a special undefined ('None') state, so there is always a representable result. Failures of flagged (checked) operations (e.g. checked-arithmetic overflow or a NaN float result) are signalled by setting st0 to false. Control flow is made total because the code is always zero-extended to 2^16 bytes, and the all-zero byte decodes to a valid opcode meaning 'set st0 to false and stop', so there are no invalid instructions and no out-of-range jumps; cycles and jumps are counted against a 2^16 limit to bound execution time.
key_points: A-registers: 8 blocks of 32 registers, widths 8/16/32/64/128/256/512/1024 bits
S-registers: one block of 256 registers, up to 64 KiB each; R-registers reserved for cryptography
Every register can hold an undefined/None state; impossible ops set destination to undefined instead of trapping
st0 is the boolean status register; flagged operations set st0=false on overflow/NaN/failure
Code is zero-padded to 2^16 bytes; the zero opcode means 'set st0=false and stop' -> no invalid instructions/jumps
Cycles and jumps are counted with a 2^16 limit for bounded-time execution

answer: LNPBP-1 commits to a message by tweaking a public key: T = Po + G * HMAC-SHA256(SHA256("LNPBP1") || SHA256(tag) || msg, S*), where Po is the chosen original key from the set, G is the secp256k1 generator, and the commitment is added to the whole keyset via S* — the 64-byte uncompressed serialization (x||y, with the 0x04 prefix stripped) of the sum S of all unique public keys controlling the output. HMAC-SHA256 is used instead of a plain hash to make arbitrary-length messages immune to length-extension attacks, and the HMAC key is S* — using the public-key sum both binds the commitment to those keys and injects entropy. The double-tagged prefix SHA256("LNPBP1") || SHA256(tag) is a BIP-340-style tagged-hash that prevents cross-protocol replay/reinterpretation. No nonce is added because the public key S already supplies enough entropy through the HMAC to defeat brute-force/dictionary attacks on short messages.
key_points: T = Po + G * HMAC-SHA256(SHA256("LNPBP1") || SHA256(tag) || msg, S*)
Commits to the SUM of all unique keys in the output, not just one key
S* is the 64-byte uncompressed sum key (x||y, 0x04 prefix stripped) and serves as the HMAC key
HMAC-SHA256 chosen to prevent length-extension attacks on arbitrary-length messages
Double SHA256 tagged prefix prevents cross-protocol collision/replay
No nonce: the public-key sum already provides sufficient entropy

answer: LNPBP-2 requires that exactly one key of all keys present in the scriptPubkey/redeemScript/witnessScript carries the LNPBP-1 tweak, but the tweak commits to the SUM of all original (pre-tweak) public keys controlling the output; committing to the sum is what makes the commitment 'deterministically singular', i.e. provably free of an alternative message under the protocol. To find keys deterministically and implementation-independently, the script is parsed with Miniscript and all pk keys are collected; if a key-hash (pk_h) is encountered that cannot be resolved to a known key the procedure fails, which blocks a multiple-commitment attack via differing extra-transaction proofs. For a Taproot output the internal (intermediate) key is tweaked rather than the output key, because tweaking the output key would break its BIP-341 commitment to the script tree and make the output unspendable. Verification needs an off-chain extra-transaction proof (ETP): the original untweaked key/keyset plus script-reconstruction data (e.g. the untweaked redeemScript/witnessScript, or the Taproot merkle-root/taptweak), which is replayed to regenerate and byte-match the scriptPubkey.
key_points: Exactly one key is tweaked, but it commits to the SUM of all original keys in the output -> deterministic singularity
Keys extracted deterministically via Miniscript parsing of the script
Procedure fails on an unresolvable pk_h to prevent multiple-commitment attacks
For P2TR the internal/intermediate key is tweaked, not the output key (else BIP-341 commitment breaks)
Verification requires an off-chain extra-transaction proof (ETP): original keys + script/taptweak reconstruction data

answer: LNPBP-4 allocates a buffer of N 32-byte slots with N much greater than the number of messages M (N is a 16-bit number, so the buffer is capped at ~2 MB). Each protocol has a unique 256-bit id, and its commitment is written into slot n = id mod N; because the position is a deterministic function of the protocol id, two commitments under the same protocol id would collide on the same slot and thus cannot both be present — which is the uniqueness guarantee. Remaining empty slots are filled with deterministic pseudo-random data: a BIP-340 tagged hash (tag "LNPBP4:entropy") of entropy_seed || j for slot index j. The whole buffer is then committed with LNPBP-1/2 using the tag "LNPBP4". A partial (per-message) reveal discloses the message, its protocol id and the full buffer, letting a verifier recompute slot n and match it — without learning the other messages. A full-disclosure reveal additionally provides entropy_seed so a verifier can regenerate every filler slot and confirm the buffer contains only the declared commitments and no hidden extra ones.
key_points: Buffer of N 32-byte slots, N >> M, capped at ~2 MB (16-bit slot count)
Each protocol has a unique 256-bit id; commitment placed at slot n = id mod N
Same-protocol-id collision on the same slot is what guarantees per-protocol uniqueness
Empty slots filled with BIP-340 tagged hash (tag 'LNPBP4:entropy') of entropy_seed||j
Final buffer committed via LNPBP-1/2 with tag 'LNPBP4'
Partial reveal proves presence; full reveal (with entropy_seed) proves absence of other commitments

answer: Opret is the simple scheme: the 32-byte MPC commitment is placed in the first OP_RETURN output of the witness transaction as 'OP_RETURN OP_PUSHBYTES_32 <mpc::Commitment>', a 34-byte script that is visible on-chain. Tapret hides the commitment inside a Taproot script tree instead, giving a smaller/indistinguishable chain footprint and better privacy. The Tapret commitment is a fixed 64-byte tapscript leaf: 29 bytes of a fixed prefix (OP_RESERVED) followed by OP_RETURN, a 33-byte push holding the 32-byte MPC commitment plus a 1-byte nonce; this leaf is inserted as an unspendable script at the first level of the tree, shifting any existing scripts one level down. Because Taproot hashes branch pairs in lexicographic order, the commitment leaf may land on the left, forcing a larger uniqueness proof that reveals sibling branches. The 1-byte nonce exists so the prover can 'mine' the leaf hash until it is greater than the rest of the tree and therefore sits on the right-hand side, which keeps the uniqueness/inclusion proof minimal and avoids revealing private sibling scripts.
key_points: Opret: 32-byte commitment in first OP_RETURN output; script = OP_RETURN OP_PUSHBYTES_32 <commit>, 34 bytes, on-chain visible
Tapret: commitment hidden in Taproot script tree for smaller footprint/better privacy
Tapret leaf is exactly 64 bytes: 29-byte fixed prefix + OP_RETURN + 33-byte push (32-byte MPC commitment + 1-byte nonce)
Tapret leaf inserted as unspendable script, shifting existing scripts down a level
Lexicographic branch ordering means left-placement needs a larger uniqueness proof
The 1-byte nonce is 'mined' so the leaf hash sorts to the right side, minimising the proof

answer: A single-use-seal is a unique object that can be 'closed' over a message exactly once. An implementation must support Close(l, m) -> w_l, producing a witness that the seal l was closed over message m, and Verify(l, w_l, m) -> bool; practical implementations also add Gen(p) -> l to generate a new seal bound to a public key (or arbitrary predicate) and an authenticated Close(l, m, s) -> w_l. The security property is that it must be infeasible for an attacker to make Verify return true for two distinct messages m1 != m2 closed over the same seal (multiple witnesses for the same seal/message pair are tolerable but non-ideal). A trivial realisation is a trusted notary that signs witnesses; the scalable, trust-minimised realisation replaces the notary with a proof-of-publication ledger whose state is agreed in a trust-minimised way — i.e. the Bitcoin blockchain, where closing a seal corresponds to spending a specified transaction output and the commitment is published on-chain.
key_points: Core ops: Close(l,m)->w and Verify(l,w,m)->bool; plus Gen(p)->l and authenticated Close(l,m,s)->w
A seal can be closed over a message exactly once
Security: infeasible to make Verify true for two distinct messages on the same seal
Multiple witnesses for the same seal/message pair are acceptable (non-ideal)
Trivial impl = trusted notary with disposable keys; trust-minimised = proof-of-publication ledger (Bitcoin)
On Bitcoin, closing a seal = spending the defined UTXO with an on-chain commitment

answer: A contract consignment is the small package needed to bootstrap a contract: it carries the contract Genesis plus its Schema (each on the order of a couple of hundred bytes, so the whole thing is typically a few KiB) and can be distributed by any channel — website, email, QR, Nostr, etc. A transfer (terminal) consignment is much larger because, in addition to the final state transition addressed to the recipient, it must include the entire validated history of state transitions back to Genesis so the receiver can independently verify the asset against the Bitcoin anchors. The receiver starts a transfer by issuing an invoice that encodes a seal definition — usually one of their UTXOs in blinded form — telling the sender where to assign the new owned state without revealing the exact outpoint. Each party keeps a 'stash' of client-side-validated data; the sender builds a PSBT/witness transaction embedding the Opret/Tapret DBC commitment (plus any 'blank' transitions for other assets on the same seal), generates the terminal consignment, and the receiver runs 'rgb accept' to validate it and merge it into their stash before the witness transaction is broadcast.
key_points: Contract consignment = Genesis + Schema, only a few KiB
Transfer/terminal consignment = final state transition + full validated history since Genesis (hence much larger)
History is needed so the receiver can verify against Bitcoin anchors client-side
Invoice encodes a seal definition, typically the receiver's UTXO in blinded form
Stash = each party's store of client-side-validated data
Sender embeds Opret/Tapret DBC in a PSBT (plus blank transitions); receiver 'rgb accept' validates before broadcast

answer: An RGB Schema is a declarative template — analogous to a class — that defines the kinds of owned state and assignments, the global state, the structure of Genesis, the permitted state transitions and their metadata, and, crucially, embeds the AluVM state-validation scripts that encode the business logic. It is compiled to a .rgb/.rgba binary and an issuer instantiates it by filling in values (ticker, name, precision, issued supply, initial allocations) in Genesis. This is fundamentally different from Ethereum, where the contract itself is executable bytecode whose state lives on-chain; in RGB the contract is purely declarative and validated client-side, with nothing but a commitment published on Bitcoin. Interfaces, introduced in v0.10, are the standardised APIs through which wallets read and act on a contract — comparable to Ethereum ABIs/ERCs — but, unlike ERCs, they need neither obligatory standardisation nor separate distribution because they travel bundled with the contract, and additional interfaces can be attached to an immutable contract over time. RGB20 is the fungible-asset interface (implemented by the NIA schema), RGB21 is for unique/collectible digital assets/NFTs (UDA), and RGB25 is for collectible fungible assets (CFA); the schema provides the implementation while the interface provides the semantic, wallet-facing view.
key_points: Schema = declarative template (like a class): owned/global state, assignments, transitions, metadata, embedded AluVM validation scripts
Issuer instantiates a schema in Genesis (ticker, precision, issued supply, allocations); compiled to .rgb/.rgba
Unlike Ethereum, the RGB contract is declarative and validated client-side; only a commitment goes on Bitcoin
Interfaces (v0.10+) are ABI/ERC-like APIs but bundled with the contract, needing no separate standardisation/distribution
Multiple interfaces can be added to an immutable contract over time
RGB20 = fungible (NIA), RGB21 = unique/NFT (UDA), RGB25 = collectible fungible (CFA)

answer: Strict types are a formal, deterministic notation for algebraic data types aimed at real computing/networking platforms rather than abstract theory. Their defining difference from Haskell/Idris-style ADTs is that every collection must carry explicit minimum and maximum bounds as part of the type itself, so resource requirements are known at compile time and runtime exceptions are avoided. They are deterministic (any two byte sequences that differ represent semantically distinct data) and impose a resource limit: no atomic encoded data piece may exceed 64 KiB, which lets even embedded/limited-memory devices process the data. Because the type system is formal, one can formally verify that (de)serialization matches a schema and prove statements about memory-layout equivalence and convertibility. RGB compiles its entire consensus layer into strict types so it can obtain compile-time size guarantees (helping hardware wallets) and, most importantly, produce formal proofs of binary compatibility between releases. Strict types were developed by Maxim Orlovsky under the UBIDECO Institute and are also used by AluVM and other client-side-validation systems.
key_points: Formal, deterministic notation for ADTs targeting real platforms, not abstract theory
Every collection has explicit min/max bounds baked into the type -> compile-time resource prediction, no runtime exceptions
Determinism: differing byte sequences always mean semantically distinct data
64 KiB rule: no atomic encoded piece may exceed 64 KiB, enabling embedded/limited-memory use
Enables formal verification of (de)serialization and memory-layout equivalence
RGB compiles its whole consensus layer to strict types for binary-compatibility proofs across releases; by Orlovsky/UBIDECO

answer: Bifrost was introduced because extending the BOLTs is painful: each atomic feature touches several separate standards, experimental features are hard to isolate from tested core code, and BOLT messaging was designed narrowly for payments — making non-payment state channels, messaging/DEX use and RGB data propagation awkward to bolt on. A central technical motivation is encoding: BOLTs use BigInt encoding, which is unsuitable for client-side-validated data, so Bifrost re-encodes all message fields with strict encoding. LNPBP-50 is the generalized networking core — it runs over TCP on a dedicated default port 9913, reuses Lightning's Noise_XK handshake/encryption and message framing (extracted as LNPBP-15/18), advertises support via a local-features flag, and defines bifrost:// URLs. On top of that core, LNPBP-51 specifies the channel-management protocol and LNPBP-53 specifies multi-peer payment channels for Bifrost (with further LNPBPs covering routed messaging, channel factories and HTLC/PTLC synchronization). Related standard LNPBP-35 defines the Bifrost message extensions used to propagate RGB data over Lightning.
key_points: Extending BOLTs is hard: features span multiple standards, no isolation of experimental code, payment-only design
BigInt encoding in BOLTs is unsuitable for client-side-validated data -> Bifrost uses strict encoding for all fields
LNPBP-50 = generalized core: TCP, dedicated default port 9913, Noise_XK (LNPBP-15) + framing (LNPBP-18), bifrost:// URLs, local-features flag
LNPBP-51 = channel-management protocol
LNPBP-53 = multi-peer payment channels for Bifrost
LNPBP-35 (related) carries RGB data propagation over Lightning

answer: Carbonado is a single flat-file archival container designed for long-term, consensus-critical data such as an RGB stash, layering several independent techniques. It applies authenticated symmetric encryption (in the v2 format, AES-256-CTR with full HMAC-SHA512 encrypt-then-MAC) to provide confidentiality and integrity of the private client-side-validated data. It uses Bao — a BLAKE3-based tree hashing scheme — to give verified streaming with per-slice (4 KiB) verifiability, so any portion can be authenticated without reading the whole file. It adds Reed-Solomon forward error correction (a deterministic 4/8 scheme) so the archive survives bit-rot and partial media loss, and optional Zstandard compression to reduce size. Newer versions also attach post-quantum (SLH-DSA / FIPS-205) signatures as optional sidecars. Together these layers target the goal of data that stays private, verifiable and recoverable over very long horizons and degraded storage — matching RGB's model where losing your client-side history means losing the asset.
key_points: Single flat-file archival container for long-term consensus-critical data (e.g. RGB stash), used by BitMask
Authenticated encryption (v2: AES-256-CTR + HMAC-SHA512 encrypt-then-MAC) for confidentiality + integrity
Bao (BLAKE3-based) verified streaming with per-4 KiB-slice verifiability
Reed-Solomon forward error correction (deterministic 4/8) against bit-rot / partial loss
Optional Zstandard compression; optional post-quantum SLH-DSA (FIPS-205) signature sidecars
Purpose: private, verifiable, recoverable data because losing client-side history loses the RGB asset

answer: The method-specific identifier is the 64-character lowercase hexadecimal x-only secp256k1 public key (the same key material as an npub, but npub bech32 is display-only, never the DID id): a DID looks like did:nostr:<64-hex>. In the minimal, network-free tier a conformant resolver MUST deterministically derive a DID document from the key alone: id set to the full DID, type "DIDNostr", a single verification method of type "Multikey", and both authentication and assertionMethod referencing that method by a relative DID URL such as "#key1". The publicKeyMultibase is constructed as multibase base16-lower (prefix "f") over the secp256k1 compressed-key multicodec varint (0xe7 0x01) followed by the parity byte and the 32-byte x-only key. Optional HTTP resolution fetches https://<domain>/.well-known/did/nostr/<pubkey>.json, and optional "enhanced" resolution queries relays for kind 0 (profile), kind 3 (follows) and kind 10002 (relay list) to enrich the document — but there is no special "DID document" event kind.
key_points: Method-specific id = 64-char lowercase hex x-only secp256k1 pubkey; npub is display-only
Minimal document is derived offline from the key alone, with type "DIDNostr"
Verification method type is "Multikey"; authentication and assertionMethod both reference #key1
publicKeyMultibase = 'f' (base16 multibase) + e701 (secp256k1 multicodec) + parity byte + hex key
Three-tier resolution: minimal (offline) -> HTTP .well-known/did/nostr/<pubkey>.json -> enhanced relay query (kind 0/3/10002); no dedicated DID-document event kind

answer: A NIP-05 identifier is the 'nip05' field on a user's kind 0 metadata event. To verify local-part@domain, the client issues a GET to https://<domain>/.well-known/nostr.json?name=<local-part> (local-part restricted to a-z0-9-_.). The response is a JSON object with a required 'names' object mapping each name to a lowercase hex public key, plus an optional 'relays' object keyed by hex pubkey giving arrays of relay URLs. The name '_' is a root identifier displayed as just the bare domain (so alice can be _@alice.com shown as 'alice.com'). Crucially, NIP-05 is only a human-friendly pointer, not an identity: clients MUST follow the public key, not the NIP-05 address — if the key behind an address changes, the client keeps the original pubkey and stops showing the now-invalid address. Servers MUST NOT return HTTP redirects and should send Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *.
key_points: Request: GET https://<domain>/.well-known/nostr.json?name=<local-part>
JSON has required 'names' (name -> lowercase hex pubkey) and optional 'relays' (pubkey -> [relay URLs])
'_' is the root identifier, displayed as the bare domain name
Security rule: clients follow the pubkey, never the NIP-05 address as primary identity
No redirects allowed; CORS header Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * recommended

answer: NIP-07 defines a window.nostr object injected by a browser extension or signer so that a web app can request Nostr operations without ever handling the user's private key — the key stays inside the extension, and the page only ever sees signatures and the pubkey. The two mandatory methods are async window.nostr.getPublicKey(): string (returns the pubkey as hex) and async window.nostr.signEvent(event): Event. signEvent receives an unsigned event object { created_at, kind, tags, content } and returns the same event completed with the id, pubkey and sig fields filled in. Optional namespaces provide encryption: window.nostr.nip04.encrypt/decrypt(pubkey, ...) (now deprecated) and window.nostr.nip44.encrypt/decrypt(pubkey, ...). Extensions typically run at document_end so window.nostr is present when pages load.
key_points: window.nostr is injected by an extension/signer so the private key never reaches the web page
getPublicKey(): returns hex pubkey
signEvent(event) takes {created_at, kind, tags, content} and returns it with id, pubkey, sig added
Optional nip04 (deprecated) and nip44 encrypt/decrypt namespaces
getRelays() optional; extension injected at document_end

answer: NIP-19 uses plain bech32 — explicitly bech32 'not-m', i.e. NOT bech32m — for all of these entities. Bare types (npub/nsec/note) are just the hex pubkey, seckey or event id re-encoded in bech32. The TLV types (nprofile/nevent/naddr, plus deprecated nrelay) pack multiple 1-byte-type / 1-byte-length / value records. The four TLV types are: 0 = special (the primary payload — a 32-byte pubkey for nprofile, a 32-byte event id for nevent, or the UTF-8 identifier 'd' string for naddr); 1 = relay (an ASCII relay URL, optional and repeatable); 2 = author (a 32-byte pubkey — required for naddr, optional for nevent); 3 = kind (a big-endian 32-bit unsigned integer). So an nprofile is an npub plus optional relay hints, telling clients where to find that person, whereas an npub is only the key. An naddr, which addresses a replaceable/addressable event, must carry the identifier (type 0), the author pubkey (type 2) and the kind (type 3), optionally with relay hints.
key_points: Uses bech32, explicitly NOT bech32m
Bare npub/nsec/note are hex re-encoded; nprofile/nevent/naddr carry TLV
TLV type 0 = special (pubkey / event id / identifier string depending on prefix)
TLV type 1 = relay (ASCII URL, repeatable); type 2 = author (32-byte pubkey); type 3 = kind (32-bit big-endian)
nprofile = pubkey + relay hints (vs bare npub); naddr must carry identifier + author + kind

answer: NIP-42 lets a relay authenticate a client. The relay initiates by sending an ["AUTH", <challenge-string>] message over the connection. The client replies with ["AUTH", <signed-event>] where the event is an ephemeral kind 22242 event (relays MUST NOT broadcast it) with created_at at the current time and at least two tags: a ["relay", "wss://..."] tag naming the target relay and a ["challenge", "..."] tag echoing the relay's challenge. The relay validates that the kind is 22242, that created_at is within a small window (~10 minutes) of now, that the challenge tag matches the challenge it issued, and that the relay tag matches its own URL. When an unauthenticated client attempts a restricted action, the relay signals it with an OK/CLOSED message prefixed 'auth-required: ' (and 'restricted: ' when the authenticated key still lacks permission).
key_points: Relay sends ["AUTH", challenge]; client returns ["AUTH", signed event]
Event is ephemeral kind 22242, never broadcast
Required tags: ["relay", url] and ["challenge", string]
Relay checks kind=22242, created_at within ~10 min, challenge match, relay URL match
'auth-required: ' prefix signals need to authenticate; 'restricted: ' for insufficient permission

answer: NIP-65 defines kind 10002, a replaceable event whose 'r' tags advertise a user's preferred relays, e.g. ["r", "wss://relay.example", "write"]. The optional third element is a marker: 'read' means a relay where the user reads (expects to receive mentions), 'write' means a relay where the user publishes; if the marker is omitted the relay is BOTH read and write. This drives the outbox/gossip model: to fetch a user's own events you query their WRITE relays, and to reach a user (mention/reply) you post to their READ relays — so followers converge on the author's own declared relays instead of everyone piling onto a few big relays. Clients should keep the list small (roughly 2-4 relays per category) and propagate the kind 10002 event widely, including to well-known indexers, so others can discover it.
key_points: kind 10002, replaceable, uses 'r' tags with relay URLs
Markers 'read' and 'write'; omitted marker means both
Fetch a user's posts from their WRITE relays; send mentions/replies to their READ relays
Underpins the outbox/gossip model (spread load onto authors' own relays)
Keep list small (~2-4 per category); propagate widely / to indexers

answer: Solid-OIDC builds on OpenID Connect Authorization Code + PKCE. The ID Token carries a 'webid' claim (the user's WebID URI) alongside 'azp' (authorized party / client) and an 'aud' that includes azp and the string 'solid'. To stop a malicious OP minting valid-looking tokens for someone else's WebID, the verifier performs WebID Provider Confirmation: it dereferences the WebID profile and checks the triple ?webid <http://www.w3.org/ns/solid/terms#oidcIssuer> ?iss, i.e. that the token's issuer is one the WebID owner actually authorised (RDF statement or Link header). Two features remove classic friction: dynamic client identity, where the OAuth Client ID is itself a dereferenceable Client ID Document (JSON-LD using the solid/oidc-context) listing redirect_uris etc., so no manual pre-registration is needed; and DPoP-bound tokens instead of bearer tokens. Per RFC 9449, the client sends a DPoP proof JWT in the 'DPoP' header — JOSE header typ='dpop+jwt', an asymmetric 'alg', and a 'jwk' public key — with payload claims jti, htm (method), htu (URI) and iat (plus 'ath', the SHA-256 of the access token, when a token is presented). The access token's 'cnf' claim then contains 'jkt' = the base64url SHA-256 JWK thumbprint of that public key, so the resource server accepts it only from the holder of the matching private key, defeating stolen-token replay.
key_points: ID Token carries webid claim, plus azp and aud including azp and 'solid'
WebID Provider Confirmation checks solid:oidcIssuer triple (http://www.w3.org/ns/solid/terms#oidcIssuer) so issuer matches WebID-authorised OP
Client ID is a dereferenceable Client ID Document (JSON-LD), removing static registration
DPoP proof JWT (RFC 9449): header typ=dpop+jwt/alg/jwk, claims jti/htm/htu/iat (+ath with a token)
Access token cnf.jkt = base64url SHA-256 JWK thumbprint binds the token to the client's DPoP key, preventing bearer-style replay

answer: Both are RDF-based, but they differ in expressiveness.
