WAC (namespace http://www.w3.org/ns/auth/acl#) is a classic ACL model: an acl:Authorization grants acl:mode values acl:Read, acl:Write, acl:Append and acl:Control (Control governs the ACL resource itself). acl:accessTo names the specific resource an authorization applies to, whereas acl:default is set on a container and is inherited by resources lower in the hierarchy that have no ACL of their own. Subjects are named with acl:agent (a specific agent), acl:agentGroup, or acl:agentClass — and public access is granted by using foaf:Agent as the agentClass (with acl:AuthenticatedAgent for any logged-in agent). The ACL resource is found via a Link header with rel="acl". ACP (namespace acp:) is attribute-/policy-based: an Access Control Resource (ACR) links a resource to acp:AccessControl objects that acp:apply acp:Policy objects; each Policy uses acp:allow/acp:deny access modes gated by acp:Matcher conditions combined with acp:allOf (AND), acp:anyOf (OR) and acp:noneOf (NOT). Crucially, matchers can test not just acp:agent but also acp:client (which application) and acp:issuer (which identity provider) and acp:vc (verifiable credentials) — contextual, attribute-based conditions WAC cannot express, since WAC decisions turn essentially on agent identity and mode alone.
key_points: WAC modes: acl:Read, acl:Write, acl:Append, acl:Control (Control = over the ACL itself)
acl:accessTo = this resource; acl:default = on a container, inherited by contained resources lacking their own ACL
Public via acl:agentClass foaf:Agent; acl:AuthenticatedAgent = any logged-in agent; ACL found via Link rel=acl
ACP: ACR -> acp:AccessControl -> acp:Policy (acp:allow/acp:deny) gated by acp:Matcher via acp:allOf/anyOf/noneOf
ACP adds attribute/context conditions on acp:client, acp:issuer and acp:vc, not just agent identity

answer: In WebID-TLS the agent presents an X.509 client certificate whose Subject Alternative Name (SAN) is a dereferenceable URI — that URI is the WebID. The verification agent extracts the WebID from the SAN, dereferences the WebID profile (RDF, e.g. Turtle), and looks for public key material attached to that WebID via cert:key (namespace http://www.w3.org/ns/auth/cert#). For an RSA key the profile carries a cert:RSAPublicKey node with a cert:modulus (xsd:hexBinary) and a cert:exponent (xsd:integer, commonly 65537). The verifier compares the modulus/exponent in the certificate against those published in the profile; a match, combined with the TLS handshake proving possession of the private key, authenticates the agent as that WebID. The community moved to WebID-OIDC / Solid-OIDC mainly for usability and reach: browser client-certificate UX is poor (confusing certificate-selection dialogs, a Firefox restart quirk, no real 'log out', awkward multiple-identity handling, unsuitable on shared/public machines), client-cert support is weak on mobile and some browsers, and it is hard for non-browser clients. WebID-OIDC keeps the WebID concept but rides mainstream OAuth2/OIDC token flows (adding WebID Provider Confirmation), giving better UX, session/logout semantics and cross-platform support.
key_points: WebID-TLS: WebID is carried in the certificate's SubjectAlternativeName (URI)
Verifier dereferences WebID profile and matches key via cert:key -> cert:RSAPublicKey with cert:modulus (hexBinary) and cert:exponent (integer)
TLS handshake proves private-key possession; key match binds cert to WebID
Moved away due to poor browser client-cert UX: confusing dialogs, no logout, multi-identity/shared-machine problems, weak mobile/browser support
Solid-OIDC keeps WebID but uses OAuth2/OIDC token flow plus WebID Provider Confirmation

answer: A client subscribes by sending an authenticated POST of a JSON-LD subscription request (context https://www.w3.org/ns/solid/notification/v1) to the subscription resource for a channel type. The request sets 'type' to the channel type and 'topic' (notify:topic) to the URL of the resource whose changes it wants. The two standard channel types live in the namespace http://www.w3.org/ns/solid/notifications# : WebSocketChannel2023 (notify:WebSocketChannel2023) and WebhookChannel2023 (notify:WebhookChannel2023). They differ in delivery direction: for a WebSocket subscription the server's response returns a receiveFrom (notify:receiveFrom) URL that the client opens a WebSocket to; for a Webhook subscription the client additionally supplies a sendTo (notify:sendTo) HTTPS URL in the request, and the server pushes notifications there (the response identifies the 'sender'). Notification payloads themselves are Activity Streams 2.0 objects serialized as JSON-LD.
key_points: Subscribe via authenticated POST of JSON-LD (context .../solid/notification/v1) to the subscription resource
Channel types in namespace http://www.w3.org/ns/solid/notifications#
WebSocketChannel2023 and WebhookChannel2023
notify:topic names the target resource; WebSocket response gives notify:receiveFrom; Webhook request supplies notify:sendTo
Notifications are Activity Streams 2.0 JSON-LD

answer: OpenTimestamps avoids one Bitcoin transaction per document by aggregation: clients send a document hash to public calendar servers, which insert it into a Merkle tree and periodically commit only the Merkle tree root into a single Bitcoin transaction (typically via an OP_RETURN output), so one transaction can anchor thousands of digests. The workflow is two-step. On 'stamp', the client hashes the file (SHA-256, with a random nonce for privacy) and receives an incomplete .ots receipt containing PendingAttestation(<calendar URL>) — it can't be verified yet because the Bitcoin transaction isn't confirmed. Later, 'upgrade' contacts the calendar and rewrites the .ots with the finished path and a BitcoinBlockHeaderAttestation, after which the proof is self-contained. A .ots proof is essentially a program: the file hash plus an ordered sequence of commitment operations (append <hex>, prepend <hex>, and hash ops such as sha256 / ripemd160) that walk from the document hash up through the Merkle tree and the Bitcoin transaction to a block's Merkle root, terminated by an attestation. Verification replays those operations starting from the document's own hash, reproduces the committed value, and checks it against the specified Bitcoin block header (needing only the file, the .ots proof and trusted block headers) — proving the document existed before that block was mined.
key_points: Calendar servers aggregate many document hashes into a Merkle tree and commit only the root to Bitcoin via OP_RETURN (one tx anchors thousands)
Two steps: stamp yields an incomplete .ots with PendingAttestation(calendar URL); upgrade adds BitcoinBlockHeaderAttestation
.ots is an ordered path of operations: append/prepend <hex> and hash ops (sha256, ripemd160)
Verification replays ops from the document hash up to the Bitcoin block Merkle root / header
Completed proof is self-contained: needs only file + .ots + trusted Bitcoin block headers
